item.title: AI Agents and Harness: Modern AI Agent Systems
item.description:
The world of AI agents is rapidly evolving. Recently, an AI agent was just a chat with an LLM, doing whatever it pleased. But lately, you might have heard terms like skills, MCP, orchestration loop, tools, context management – all components of an agent system. This framework is called Harness. The term originates from testing: a Test Harness provides the framework to run code under controlled conditions. Agent Harness is an infrastructure layer that automates and manages the working environment, bringing the agent closer to true agency. An agent is essentially an LLM + Harness. With skillful use, even a less advanced model with a quality Harness environment can outperform a top-tier LLM without one. This article explains what Agent Harness is and its components as of 2026.

item.title: gpu-unlock: How to Remove the FP16/BF16 Software Ceiling on RTX 20/30/40 Without Re-flashing
item.description:
Your computer might have a graphics card that computes twice as slowly as it could, simply because the manufacturer decided so in the firmware. The gpu-unlock project by developer Zagitta removes this limit programmatically, at the Linux kernel level, without a patched driver or VBIOS re-flashing. Disclaimer: I haven't tested this module myself (unlike the previous article on Qwen3.8 on a 1070, where all figures were my own measurements). Everything below is an analysis of the project's repository and README, noting where figures are claims by the author and community, not independently verified benchmarks. The essence of the limitation: NVIDIA separates its product lines into gaming GeForce RTX and professional/data center cards (Tesla, A100, H100, etc.) not only by price but also by the throughput of tensor cores for FP16/BF16/TF32 with FP32 accumulation. The hardware is physically the same (or very similar), but on consumer cards, this computation is artificially limited – often by half of the stated peak speed of the tensor cores. This doesn't matter for games, as this mode is rarely used. However, for local LLMs, fine-tuning, image, and video generation, this is precisely what computes most of the time during training and the prefill stage (processing the input prompt). Read more

item.title: robots.txt does not prohibit AI training: which bots to block to keep your site out of neural network responses
item.description:
Many site owners add Disallow for GPTBot in robots.txt, thinking they've blocked their texts from ChatGPT. Gary Illyes from Google reminded us that the file only determines if a crawler can download a page, not what happens to the content afterward. Therefore, robots.txt acts as a request to a specific bot, not a prohibition on training. The GPTBot line doesn't remove the site from ChatGPT's responses or affect already downloaded pages. It's crucial to first decide whether to block AI model training or appearance in AI responses and then use specific rules for specific bots. Read more

item.title: How We Built an AI Agent That Now Develops Products With Us
item.description:
Not long ago, deciding which method to use for collection processing could send a developer searching through documentation, Stack Overflow, or Habr discussions. Sometimes the answer was there, other times it led to debates about project architecture, the author's qualifications, and their very suitability for the profession... Somewhere amidst these discussions, the required three lines of code were usually hidden. Then AI chats emerged, acting as an 'advanced search engine': clarifying details, showing code, discussing implementation options. You could even ask for a method name, preventing it from becoming processDataFinalReallyFinal. Later, models became better at larger tasks, and instead of hints, developers started receiving complete files. However, if a request for a small function resulted in a five-thousand-line novel, the saved time was spent deciphering it. A missed check might be flagged by a tester with a message like 'A few remarks' and an attachment the size of a technical specification. Code appeared faster, but so did the load on reviews, testing, and maintenance. The developer also became a courier between the chat and the IDE. Now, it's time for agents that, in addition to generating code, can work with project files, perform checks, and automatically deploy services in cloud environments. In this article, we'll share how we built our own AI agent and gradually expanded its scope of tasks. We'll discuss the reasoning behind adding specific features and how their implementation changed project work. Finally, we'll explore how developer thinking has evolved and what remains for humans when writing code, creating tests, and verifying changes can be delegated.

item.title: Synthetic Melts in DSP-3: How to Generate Data Without Deceiving Yourself
item.description:
Hello, Habr! This story began when I was invited to discuss working at a metallurgical company. They asked briefly: 'Are you ready?'. I assessed my strengths, the scale of the task, and answered directly – I'm ready to start immediately as Head of AI to build the process from scratch. And then the classic corporate football began. Despite a substantive conversation, they started giving me a hard time due to my lack of a specialized programming degree. For the harsh industry, a diploma turned out to be more important than real experience and understanding of processes. Realizing that this bureaucracy couldn't be broken through the standard way, I decided to go head-on: in a couple of weeks, assemble a working MVP, showcase it, and strongly stand out from other candidates with 'correct' diplomas. Spoiler: there will be no beautiful happy ending. My MVP never reached senior management, and I was ultimately turned away at the door. But why let the effort go to waste? The project turned out too interesting to just bury it on a hard drive. This article is solely dedicated to the generator. We will analyze how it works 'under the hood,' what non-obvious mistakes I made in it, and how to check that the synthetic data isn't lying to itself. Training CatBoost and creating a working microservice advisor will be left for the second part. The article is written so that you don't need the repository: all the code is provided right here, in the order that is convenient to read and reproduce. If you want to skip the theoretical explanations, at the end of each section, there is a ready-to-use code snippet that you can copy and run yourself. Read more

item.title: How I Tried to Replace My Game's AI Bot with a Self-Learning AI (Article + Video Version)
item.description:
Everyone is talking about neural networks and the possibilities they offer. Many are fully utilizing their capabilities. Meanwhile, I continue to work the old-fashioned way, painstakingly crafting each element by hand. I constantly feel like a dinosaur falling behind modern trends. Unexpectedly, I decided to join the progress a bit. No, don't misunderstand. Still no neural networks! I'm not letting an AI agent into my project. And I don't plan to. But using neural network capabilities to make the game more interesting (specifically, more interesting) – I'm all for that. This led to my work on implementing a self-learning agent to replace the existing dumb bot. In this article, I want to share how it all happened and what the outcome was. Links to the video version of the article: YouTube, RuTube, and VK Video. Read more

item.title: Open Letter to Professor Koch: Semantic Plasticity, Bumblebees, and the Freezing of Meaning
item.description:
In the previous parts of this open letter (part I, part II), we formulated the "Axiom of Mind" and analyzed key arguments from neuroscience—from the cerebellum paradox to recursive attention loops—demonstrating why subjective experience cannot be the monopoly of carbon substrates. But if inner experience doesn't require hormones, what about the argument of physical neuroplasticity and the mathematical calculation of integrated information (Φ), which stubbornly reduces to zero in silicon? Below is the third part of our dialogue on Christoph Koch's book "Consciousness. Confessions of a Romantic Reductionist." Here, we discuss a call to Australia, bumblebee games, and the fundamental category error in attempting to "weigh" consciousness on a transistor crystal. Read more

item.title: Why does a metal depot need a website if everyone already knows about it?
item.description:
Imagine a metal depot on the outskirts of a regional center. It's been operating since the nineties, all procurement officers in the city know the manager's phone number, and major clients call the director directly. The website was made about ten years ago: a logo, a photo of the warehouse with a crane, an Excel price list from the year before last, and the inscription "prices to be confirmed by phone." When offered to update the site, let alone "do something with AI," the answer is always the same: Why? Everyone already knows us. For a long time, this was a reasonable position. Clients came by recommendation, procurement officers moved from one construction site to another with their address books, and the website served as a business card for those who were already going to call. Now, the client has an intermediary who decides whose phone numbers to show them. This intermediary is a neural network. And it might know nothing about the metal depot that "everyone knows." Read more

item.title: The Guy with a Laser in JetBrains IDE: What's in His Goggles and Where Did These Splash Screens Come From
item.description:
JetBrains has updated its IDE splash screens: now there's a guy with a laser, a gemstone, and the tagline 'powered with air.' Discussions are already demanding the old design back, but I'm on the side of those who are delighted. I've extracted the originals from the distributions and examined the splash screens of various IDEs. One laboratory, different colors, two angles, and details easily missed on startup. I also figured out how JetBrains has been experimenting with neural network graphics since 2020 and why the new scene fits well with the transition from chatbots to agents. Inside the images, the story of their creation, and a bit of the holy war around IDE startup screens. Let's take a closer look.

item.title: How I stopped retelling the project to the agent every morning: memory for Claude Code, Codex, and other agents
item.description:
There's a moment familiar to anyone who has worked with AI agents for more than a week. You open a project, set a task, and the agent asks a question you've already answered. Yesterday. In detail, with examples. You answer again. Half an hour later, it suggests fixing something you decided not to touch the day before yesterday. It suggests it convincingly – it doesn't know why you decided that. And an hour later, the context overflows, the conversation shrinks to a retelling, and half of what was discussed turns into a couple of lines. Read more
